newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan pledges biggest shakeup in U.N. history.
newsitem.headline: Annan pledges biggest shakeup in U.N. history.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan proposed the biggest shakeup in the history of the United Nations on Wednesday, pledging to overhaul its bureaucracy, shrink budgets, merge programmes and put the savings to work in poor nations.
"This is my pledge to you and to the world: that starting today, we begin a quiet revolution in the United Nations," Annan told the General Assembly in introducing his report.
In the 90-page document, he said the United Nations was becoming increasingly "fragmented, duplicative and rigid," often unable to meet expectations with accomplishments.

But he told the Assembly: "This is the age of the United Nations. There is a light at the end of our century's dark and dangerous tunnel, and it is brightened by the hopes and dreams of all the world's people. The United Nations remains the one, true and universal vessel of those dreams."

For some, particularly critics in the U.S. Congress, the revolution may be too quiet. No single proposal is striking on its own, but the combination of complicated reforms is expected to change the way the world body does business.

Annan's new plans build on reforms announced since he took office in January -- removing 1,000 jobs from the budget, holding spending to $1.3 billion a year, cutting administrative costs from 38 percent to 25 percent, and reducing paperwork by 40 percent by the end of the year.
There are no wholesale firings. With the average staff age at 49, half of the 9,000 employees in the secretariat or the main bureaucracy will be retiring in the next 10 years.

"Judge us not only by the cuts we propose or by the structures we change," he said. "Judge us instead -- and judge us rightly -- by the relief and the refuge that we provide to the poor, the hungry, the sick and threatened, the peoples of the world whom the United Nations exists to serve."

Annan recommended appointment of a deputy secretary-general, expected to be a woman, the creation of a cabinet that would cut by a third the 27 senior officials reporting to him and the merging of several departments.

In an apparent effort to get the support of the Third World, which holds a majority in the General Assembly, Annan proposed that savings -- expected to reach $200 million by 2002 -- be put in a new fund for economic assistance programmes for poor nations.

The U.S. Senate is moving toward appropriating $819 million of the $1.6 billion in arrears owed to the United Nations. Conditions are attached to the U.S. payment -- many of which the United Nations can meet but some of which are opposed by the rest of the world as eccentric.

In his initial reaction, U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson called Annan's proposals a "significant step" that would enable the United Nations to do "more for the world's people, to do it better and to do it for less."

The proposals create a cabinet in four groupings -- peace and security; economic and social affairs; development; and humanitarian affairs -- and thereby downgrade administration and support services in major decision-making.

Human rights issues will get a higher profile in the cabinet and under a new plan to put the Geneva-based Centre for Human Rights under Irish President Mary Robinson, who will become U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights.

The new plan groups the U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF), the U.N. Population Fund and the U.N. Development Programme (UNDP) under the chairmanship of UNDP director Gustave Speth for coordination purposes. But it does not change the structure of the agencies.
Plans were dropped to abolish the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs, which has been unable to coordinate the stronger individual agencies but is a favourite among Europeans.
It will be replaced by a smaller relief coordinator's office and represent the Geneva-based U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, the World Food Programme and others in the cabinet.
